title: Static vs Dynamic Layouts in CuTe DSL
key_concepts: Hybrid approach for balancing static and dynamic benefits
critical_patterns: Use static layouts for fixed problem sizes and performance-critical kernels
Use dynamic layouts for arbitrary input sizes and many size variants
Hybrid approach: Static inner dimensions, dynamic outer dimensions
Use cute.assume() to optimize dynamic code
constraints: Static layouts require recompilation for different sizes
Dynamic layouts have runtime address calculation overhead
Static layouts are less flexible and have more compilation overhead
Dynamic layouts may be slightly slower due to less aggressive optimization
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL supports both static and dynamic layouts, each with distinct advantages and trade-offs. Static layouts, where shape and stride are known at compile time, allow for better optimization, such as loop unrolling and constant propagation, resulting in faster execution. However, they require recompilation for different sizes, making them less flexible and increasing compilation overhead. Dynamic layouts, with shape and stride determined at runtime, offer flexibility and faster compilation, but may incur a slight performance penalty due to runtime address calculation and less aggressive compiler optimization. The choice between static and dynamic layouts depends on the specific use case: static layouts are ideal for fixed problem sizes and performance-critical kernels, while dynamic layouts are suitable for arbitrary input sizes and scenarios with many size variants. A hybrid approach, using static inner dimensions and dynamic outer dimensions, can provide a balance of performance and flexibility. Developers can use `cute.assume()` to help the compiler optimize dynamic code without runtime overhead. Static layouts are particularly beneficial for memory-bound kernels, while dynamic layouts are often sufficient for compute-bound kernels. Profiling is recommended to determine the actual performance impact before optimizing. Compilation strategies include generating one static kernel per size, using one dynamic kernel for all sizes, or a hybrid strategy where common sizes use static kernels and uncommon sizes fall back to dynamic kernels. Best practices involve using static layouts for performance-critical inner loops, profiling before optimizing, and leveraging assumptions to aid dynamic code optimization. Avoid over-specializing with static layouts when dynamic would suffice and be mindful of compilation time when generating numerous static variants.
